title: Cap. VIII: Garissoles darkens Calvin — Placeus leaves the reader to judge
pass_a_gloss: Even so, Garissoles tries to throw darkness on a passage that is so clear. He says those words do not deny that we die by Adam's own actual sin — and Placeus does not deny that either, and never has. What the words mark, he says, is that Adam's sin must not be cut off from our corruption, because the same guilt rises from both. Whether the words mean that, and whether that is the reason given, the Reader may judge. For me this is enough:
pass_b_english: Yet D. Garissoles tries to cast darkness over a place so clear. "By which words," he says, "it is not denied that we perish by Adam's own actual sin" — and Placeus neither denies this nor has ever denied it — "but it is signified that that sin of Adam is not to be parted from our corruption, seeing that from both the same guilt rises together." Whether those words signify that, and whether that reason is brought, let judgment rest with the Reader. This is enough for me:
source_text: Conatur tamen tam claro loco tenebras offundere D. G. Quibus verbis, inquit, non negatur nos Adami ipsius actuali peccato perire, nec hoc etiam negat, aut negavit unquam Placeus: Sed significatur, non esse illud Adami peccatum a nostra corruptione separandum, quippe cum ex utroque confurgat idem reatus. An id verbis illis significetur, eaque ratio afferatur, iudicium esto penes Lectorem. Illud mihi satis est,
